source.title_on_document: My Way or the AI Way? How Autonomy Frustration Undermines Creative Performance Through Editing AI Advice

supplement.where: Online Supporting Information section of the Wiley article, https://doi.org/10.1111/caim.70090 (listed on p. 14); not included in the PDF on file. The paper describes https://osf.io/qyvj8/overview as holding the quantitative data of the main study and manipulation check (p. 5; p. 10). The online supplement and posted data were not inspected in this finalization.
supplement.holds: The p. 14 listing describes Figure S1 as a box plot of DAT scores across the human, human-ChatGPT-4, and ChatGPT-4 groups including Tukey HSD group differences, and Table S1 as mediation results without covariates. Footnote 5 (p. 10) refers to Supporting Information for detailed group-comparison results; p. 7 refers there for the mediation without control variables. The main PDF does not print a direct human-ChatGPT versus human-alone statistic or the human-alone DAT mean and SD. Whether the supplement gives exact arm means, SDs, or additional standard errors is unverified.

paper_design_summary: A qualitative prestudy interviewed 26 working graduate students in Germany about autonomy when using AI (p. 5, Section 3.1.1). The main study analyzed 377 German university students who completed the Divergent Association Task (DAT): 222 chose a fixed, editable ChatGPT-4 list of 10 words and 155 declined it; an algorithm scored their final word lists, the main mediation analysis used the 222 who chose AI advice, and a footnote compared both human groups with ChatGPT-4 alone (pp. 5-7, Sections 4.1-4.2; p. 10, footnote 5). A separate manipulation check analyzed self-reported decision-making autonomy with and without AI advice for 88 students who chose AI advice, from 120 remaining after exclusions (p. 6, Section 4.1.3).

studies.label: Main study (DAT with optional, self-selected ChatGPT-4 advice)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was randomly assigned. Before the DAT, each participant chose whether to receive a fixed ChatGPT-4-generated list of 10 words that they could edit, or to generate their own 10 words.
assignment.quote: Before beginning the DAT, participants were given the option to receive AI-generated advice from ChatGPT-4 (OpenAI 2023). Participants who chose to receive the AI advice (N = 222) were presented with a set of 10 AI-generated words

arms.name: AI advice (self-selected; human-ChatGPT)
arms.description: Shown a fixed set of 10 ChatGPT-4-generated words (horizon, planet, notebook, honesty, chimpanzee, cake, plateau, opera, airplane, gloves) and allowed to edit any number of them before finalizing; then reported autonomy frustration.

arms.name: No AI advice (self-selected; human alone)
arms.description: Opted out of AI advice and generated their own list of 10 words.

arms.name: ChatGPT-4 alone (AI output benchmark, no participants)
arms.description: Not a group of people: ChatGPT-4 was prompted with the standardized DAT instructions and produced 100 unique solutions (M = 85.62, SD = 3.42; p. 10, footnote 3). Footnote 5 reports a ChatGPT-4-alone condition in an ANOVA, but does not identify which or how many AI solutions were analyzed there; the generated-solution count must not be treated as the ANOVA sample size.

participants.exclusions: 397 recruited; no multivariate outliers (Mahalanobis distance, cutoff p = 0.001); 20 excluded for missing data; 377 analyzed (222 chose AI advice, 155 did not). The paper does not say which option the 20 excluded people had chosen. The mediation analysis uses only the 222 who chose AI advice (p. 5, Section 4.1.1; group sizes p. 6; Tables 1 and 2, p. 7, N = 222).
participants.who: Students from three large German universities, mostly in part-time (dual) degree courses while employed; recruited through an online portal for course credit; 77.5% female, mean age 24.84 (SD 5.33); average 26.19 h of work per week.
participants.quote: We excluded 20 participants due to missing data, resulting in a final sample of 377 participants
participants.locator: p. 5, Section 4.1.1; group sizes p. 6, Section 4.1.1

ai_tool.how_used: Participants who opted in saw one fixed AI-generated 10-word DAT solution and could edit any number of the words before submitting; there was no live interaction with the chatbot. The solution was the one of 100 ChatGPT-4 solutions with the smallest absolute deviation from their mean (M = 85.62, SD = 3.42); the paper prints X = 85.64 beside it (footnote 3, p. 10).

task.description: Divergent Association Task (Olson et al. 2021): produce 10 single English nouns as different from each other as possible in all meanings and uses; the score is the transformed average pairwise semantic distance among the first seven valid words, computed by an algorithm.

outcomes.name: DAT score: human-ChatGPT group (chose AI advice) vs human-alone group (opted out)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: DAT score: transformed average pairwise semantic distance among the first seven valid words of each participant's final list, computed by algorithm (p. 6, Section 4.1.2.2); it scores the spread of meanings among one person's own words. Groups are self-selected. The PDF reports a one-way ANOVA across the human-alone, human-ChatGPT, and ChatGPT-4-alone groups (p. 10, footnote 5) and lists Supporting Information Figure S1 as a box plot including Tukey HSD group differences (p. 14). Table 1 prints the DAT mean only for the AI-advice group (N = 222). The direct pairwise statistic is not printed in this PDF; Figure S1 itself was not inspected.

contrasts.reported: No statistic for this pair is printed in the PDF. The p. 14 listing describes Supporting Information Figure S1 as a box plot including Tukey HSD group differences; the figure is online and was not inspected. Footnote 5 prints each human group against the same ChatGPT-4-alone condition: human-alone ΔM = –7.94, 95% CI [–9.36, –6.52]; human-ChatGPT collaboration ΔM = –4.08, 95% CI [–5.51, –2.65] (all p < 0.001); omnibus one-way ANOVA F(2, 402) = 87.24, p < 0.001. Table 1: AI-advice group DAT M = 82.87, SD = 4.51, N = 222; human-alone mean and SD not printed. Direction implied by the two differences against the same reference. Groups self-selected.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, footnote 5; p. 7, Table 1; p. 14, Supporting Information (Figure S1)

outcomes.name: DAT score within the AI-advice group: extent of editing and autonomy frustration (mediation)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same DAT score. PROCESS Model 4 (OLS paths, 5000 bootstrap resamples) with self-reported autonomy frustration (3-item METUX TENS-task subscale, 7-point, omega = 0.70) as predictor and extent of editing (number of the 10 AI words edited, 0 to 10) as mediator; covariates gender, age, education, weekly working hours, and prior ChatGPT use; N = 222 participants who chose AI advice. Results without covariates are in Supporting Information Table S1 (not in this PDF). A correlational analysis within one self-selected group, not an arm contrast.

contrasts.treatment_arm: More AI words edited (extent of editing, continuous 0 to 10, within the AI-advice group)
contrasts.control_arm: Fewer AI words edited (continuous, within the AI-advice group; no separate arm)
contrasts.reported: Path b (extent of editing -> DAT): B = −0.621, SE = 0.053, p < 0.001, 95% CI [−0.727, −0.515]; Table 1 correlation of extent of editing with DAT r = −0.62 (p < 0.001). Path c′ (autonomy frustration -> DAT, direct): B = 0.100, SE = 0.208, p = 0.630, 95% CI [−0.310, 0.511]. Indirect effect of autonomy frustration via extent of editing (a × b): B = −0.403, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.721, −0.084]; R² = 0.404. Path a (autonomy frustration -> extent of editing, not a DAT outcome): B = 0.650, SE = 0.262, p = 0.014, 95% CI [0.134, 1.17]. Table 1 (N = 222): DAT M = 82.87, SD = 4.51; extent of editing M = 5.04, SD = 4.54; autonomy frustration M = 2.78, SD = 1.18, r with DAT = −0.06. Estimates nonstandardized.

outcomes.name: DAT score: ChatGPT-4-alone benchmark vs the two self-selected human groups
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Same DAT score. AI-generated DAT solutions compared with the human-alone and human-ChatGPT groups in the footnote 5 one-way ANOVA; the p. 14 listing describes Tukey HSD group differences in Supporting Information Figure S1. Footnote 3 reports 100 ChatGPT-4 solutions generated and scored (M = 85.62, SD = 3.42). The analyzed group sizes for the ANOVA are not stated, so n_units is null; the reported F(2, 402) does not transparently reconcile with the human sample counts and the generated-solution count. One observation is one DAT solution, whether submitted by a participant or generated by ChatGPT-4. Answers none of the three questions: one contrast is AI output versus human output, the other human-AI collaboration versus AI alone (p. 10, footnotes 3 and 5; pp. 5-6, Section 4.1.1).

contrasts.control_arm: ChatGPT-4 alone (AI output benchmark, no participants)
contrasts.reported: Printed as human-ChatGPT collaboration group minus ChatGPT-4 alone: ΔM = –4.08, 95% CI [–5.51, –2.65], p < 0.001 (post hoc comparison after the omnibus one-way ANOVA F(2, 402) = 87.24, p < 0.001). No SE printed. Human-ChatGPT group DAT M = 82.87, SD = 4.51, N = 222 (Table 1); 100 ChatGPT-4 solutions M = 85.62, SD = 3.42 (footnote 3). The PDF does not establish that the Table 1 sample and footnote 3 AI reference are exactly those used in the footnote 5 ANOVA; the discrepancy remains open.

eligibility.reason: The main study fails criterion 1: participants chose whether to receive ChatGPT-4 advice (222 chose it, 155 declined; pp. 5-6, Section 4.1.1). It meets criterion 2 with 377 people analyzed after 20 exclusions (p. 5, Section 4.1.1), and criterion 3 because an algorithm scored the semantic distances in participants' final DAT word lists (p. 6, Section 4.1.2.2). It is quasi_people, retained as observational context; the human-alone versus ChatGPT-4-alone benchmark is AI-versus-human context (p. 10, footnote 5). The qualitative prestudy has 26 interviewees and no output-scored outcome (p. 5, Section 3). The manipulation check analyzes 88 people; condition-order randomization is not stated, and its only reported outcome is self-reported autonomy, so it fails criterion 3 regardless of the unresolved order (p. 6, Section 4.1.3). No study meets all three criteria.

one_line_finding: Among the 222 German students who chose to receive and edit a fixed ChatGPT-4 solution to the Divergent Association Task, each additional AI word edited was associated with a 0.621-point lower DAT score (SE = 0.053, p < 0.001; p. 7, Table 2), and in the self-selected comparison the human-alone and human-ChatGPT groups scored 7.94 and 4.08 points below ChatGPT-4 alone (95% CIs [–9.36, –6.52] and [–5.51, –2.65]; p. 10, footnote 5), with no direct human-ChatGPT versus human-alone statistic in the PDF.
open_questions: The analyzed group sizes in the footnote 5 ANOVA are not stated. Its F(2, 402) does not transparently reconcile with the 222 AI-advice and 155 no-AI participants and the 100 AI solutions generated in footnote 3; the latter is not a confirmed ANOVA count (pp. 5-6, Section 4.1.1; p. 10, footnotes 3 and 5).

The Table 1 AI-advice DAT mean (82.87), footnote 3 AI mean (85.62), and footnote 5 human-ChatGPT-minus-AI difference (-4.08) do not reconcile. The PDF does not identify whether this reflects different analysis samples or references, or a reporting error (p. 7, Table 1; p. 10, footnotes 3 and 5).

The main PDF gives neither the human-alone DAT mean and SD nor a direct human-ChatGPT versus human-alone statistic. Figure S1 is described as a box plot with Tukey HSD group differences, but its exact contents were not inspected; the paper also links the quantitative data at https://osf.io/qyvj8/overview (p. 14, Supporting Information; p. 10, footnote 5 and Data Availability Statement).
The main study does not say whether the 20 participants excluded for missing data had chosen AI advice (p. 5, Section 4.1.1).
The manipulation check does not say how the without-AI and with-AI condition order was assigned, or which AI model and advice were used for this separate sample (p. 6, Section 4.1.3).
notes: Study IDs follow both screeners: S1 prestudy, S2 main study, S3 manipulation check. This form replaces an earlier reconciled form of 2026-10-05, which numbered the manipulation check S2 and the main study S3. The ethics statement refers to 'the three studies' (p. 10). No preregistration and no random assignment are mentioned anywhere in the PDF. Every opt-in participant saw the same fixed ChatGPT-4 list of 10 words, and no diversity outcome is reported. Autonomy frustration (self-report) and extent of editing (number of AI words changed, a behavioral process measure) exist only for the AI-advice group and are not listed as outcomes. The three S2 outcome entries share one DAT score; they are split so that each entry's question, sample, AI availability, and primary status hold for all its contrasts. In S2-O3 the paper prints each difference as human group minus ChatGPT-4 alone; the contrast orientation follows the screeners. The manipulation check used a sample different from the main study (p. 6, Section 4.1.3), and no overlap with other papers is stated. Final review: no c033 challenge files were present, so challenge-resolution counts are zero. The complete markdown was read, including references and the Supporting Information listing; recorded empirical numbers were checked against PDF pp. 5-7 and 10. No separate appendix is included in this PDF. Final specification clarifications label analyzed counts, distinguish generated AI solutions from unknown ANOVA units, and avoid claiming uninspected supplement contents. S3 assignment.randomized is now not_stated because its assigned unit is within-person order and that order is unreported; the self-selection of advice remains explicit. This clarification supersedes the historical S3 randomization resolution, while the reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as requested. The S3 order question affects criterion 1 for that study but cannot make it core-eligible without a reported output-scored outcome.

open_items.item: ANOVA group sizes and which generated AI solutions were analyzed (p. 10, footnotes 3 and 5) need author clarification. This affects numerical extraction, not an eligibility criterion: the main human analysis already exceeds the people threshold and AI choice was self-selected.

The incompatible DAT mean/reference/mean-difference reports (p. 7, Table 1; p. 10, footnotes 3 and 5) need clarification of the analyzed samples or correction of a reporting error. This affects the reported comparison, not any eligibility criterion.

Human-alone DAT mean and SD are absent from the main PDF; participant-level scores and group labels in the posted main-study data would settle them. This affects numerical extraction, not the confirmed output-scoring or people-count criteria (p. 10, Data Availability Statement).
The direct human-ChatGPT versus human-alone Tukey HSD result requires inspecting Supporting Information Figure S1, described on p. 14. Its significance does not affect any eligibility criterion.

AI-advice choices of the 20 people excluded for missing data are unreported (p. 5, Section 4.1.1); the authors could provide the exclusion breakdown. This does not affect the criteria: the analyzed human counts are explicit and comfortably exceed the threshold.

Randomization of the manipulation-check condition order is not stated (p. 6, Section 4.1.3). An author-provided procedure or allocation record would settle criterion 1 for S3. This cannot change the final core exclusion because S3 reports only self-reported autonomy and fails criterion 3.

The manipulation-check AI model and exact advice are not identified (p. 6, Section 4.1.3); its study materials from the authors would settle this descriptive detail. A specific model name is not required by an eligibility criterion, and S3 has no reported output-scored outcome.
